en: It is the heirloom left by your forefather,
Tested before all the people,
A cherished delight and faithful companion.
If one possessed no weapon such as this,
How could he strike a distant mark?
It is the companion of mortal life;
That is the weapon for charging and firing,
That is the sharp arm your forefather left.
When they trampled and scattered our wealth,
And broke open my treasury,
Whoever its bullet struck lost blood,
And with the blood, life itself departed.
Its cartridge pouch bristled with bullets;
The enemies who came to confront it
Suffered for their folly and fell.
When it was aimed toward the foe,
The earth was torn and blood flowed.
When fired it cracked like a beast’s roar,
Smoke curled from its barrel,
And the opposing enemy collapsed.
The fearsome musket Akkelte—
Its fiery bullets are large as fists;
Such is the nature of Akkelte.
They faced the foe and raised it,
And when it fired, it ended lives.
Its bullet struck whatever it marked,
And the enemy caught in its path
Was hurled into utter darkness.
If its bullet struck squarely,
The enemy could find no escape,
Nor gather bones scattered like flies,
If ever caught by its shot.
They grieved, unable to find the remains.
Akkelte strikes from afar;
When foes heard Akkelte’s voice,
And its bullet struck with a crash,
Even the bravest enemy lost courage
And fled away in panic.
None could resist or hold firm;
They were shattered and torn apart.
Its match is red silk and glowing ember;
No gun on earth is like it.
Steel within and gold without,
Its barrel is twisted with twelve grooves.
The foe it was aimed at fell,
No enemy could stand against it,
At every winding ridge it found its mark.
Any slight flaw was corrected
By the smith Döötü and poor Bölökbai;
No other sharp weapon was like it.
He gathered his young warriors
And named them the Forty Companions.
Finding no land left to raid,
On this side of Kakan,
In the open country of Kaspan-Tоо,
Along the ridge of Altyn-Tоо,
In the lifeless, barren desert,
He encountered it by providence:
Zulpukor, descended from the heavens,
Was found there by chance
For your gray-maned heroic forefather.
Knowing it would bring great slaughter,
He adorned its hilt with gold,
And the saintly elder, brave Bakai,
Gave it the name Zulpukor.
Zulpukor is a keen, fiery sword;
When wielded against a facing foe,
When swung against a vaunting enemy,
It reddens and bursts into flame,
And when struck at an encountered foe,
It lengthens to forty fathoms.
Whomever its edge touches is gone;
When it is swung, life departs.
Its edge does not catch as it cuts,
Its touch is scarcely felt,
Until the victim falls and blood flows.
When it strikes stone, dust erupts;
When it strikes sand, fire leaps forth.
No enemy dared face it,
And if some boastful foe
Chanced to attack it head-on,
Not one of his lineage survived.
When drawn screaming from its sheath,
It yearned to drink blood;
No living soul who clashed with it
Returned safely to his family.
If you would strike, that is the keen blade;
Passing down since your forefather’s time,
That is the treasured heirloom,
The sharp blade handed down from old.
When they pressed down upon my head,
When they drove off all my livestock,
When they seized my gold and left me grieving,
And entered to plunder the royal camp,
Only a blue dress remained upon my back.
I had no son behind me,
And no strength to fight them.
The world turned to filth and emptiness,
And my Akkelte remained
In the hands of the dog Kanchoro.
He ruined all my days;
Listen, my son, to my sorrow.
Go to that rabid slave
And ask him to return as your inheritance
The possessions of your gray-maned father.
If he refuses to give them as your inheritance,
Return without quarreling,
And come tell wretched me,
“Kanchoro refused to give them.”
There is a wondrous matter I must tell;
Listen without grieving, my son.
That single precious object
Is worth all the livestock beneath the sky;
Such is this honored treasure—
My orphaned darling, heed me well.
Your earliest forefather, your great grandsire,
Grew up and was born in Altai,
Then stirred the whole world.
Red and green flames burned,
And his worth became known among the people.
The prowess of that gray-maned hero
Was inscribed among all nations.
At twelve he conquered a royal camp
And rode against a realm with its own court;
His fame spread across the world
And was entered in the chronicle
Of the khan of Kakan city.
He tended white stallions and gathered steeds,
Swiftly assembled valiant men,
And slaughtered ninety beasts for his feast.
A saint unlike ordinary men.
Go slaughter the gray beast,
And at the funeral feast, my orphan,
Eat until you are fully satisfied,
Then lay him in a place of honor.
Remember these solemn words;
My hero, my son, heed my counsel.
Your grandmother Kanykey
Was a great and holy woman;
That we were parted from the saint
Was a fate ordained by God.
Weeping and grieving in disgrace,
My darling, we were left behind,
Torn away from our motherland,
From my black-walled city with its gates,
From my village pitched upon the river terrace,
From the homeland that sustained me,
And from the angelic purity
Of my heroic mother.
I wailed aloud in grief,
And while my frail life yet clung sweetly,
I was parted from my true mother.
I screamed and wept till the pasture rang,
Enduring disgrace and bondage.
They dealt me a cruel fate
And slashed my breast open.
My two eyes rolled wildly,
My arms and legs hung limp;
Your fierce mother was bound,
And my two eyes wept a pasture of tears.
My blood drained away as I choked,
My poor coat was torn apart.
As I screamed in grief,
I was parted from my towering protector.
While I suffered plunder,
They cut down my banner with swords,
Hewed down my fruit with axes,
Trampled my living body underfoot,
Struck me heedless of my fury,
And reduced my days to a mere handful.
No hero could withstand that blade,
Nor could any man equal it;
Its steel nature was plain to see,
And two foes who faced it were cleft apart.
When enemies came face-to-face with it,
Their blood was spilled.
Know that such was Zulpukor:
When it unleashed tumult,
Its very blade became invisible,
While the hostile enemy’s coats and robes
Were taken away as plunder.
Upon the broad ridges of Talas,
The keen steel blade was left behind
In the hands of accursed Kanchoro.
Go gather and bring back your inheritance;
Say, “These are the possessions left by my father,”
And demand them from that treacherous dog.
If he will not heed your words,
If he refuses what you are to receive,
Come and tell wretched me,
“Mother, he refused to give it,”
And return without trading insults.
If you have the strength, go
To your aged grandsire Bakai,
And saying, “You are my inherited legacy,”
Bring your poor aged grandsire
Back here with you.
If by chance he has died,
If he has suddenly left this world,
If your grandsire has passed away,
Your elder, the hero Bakai,
Bend him gently, holding him at the waist,
And load him upon the gray beast.
If the chance is yours,
If you find a solitary place,
Choose a fitting spot and dig his grave,
Dedicate and slaughter the gray beast,
And with your own hands
Mark your grandsire’s grave and lay him there.
Your grandsire, the aged Bakai—
I drew it from its sheath.
When they pressed hard upon me,
When those accursed Jediger
Came surging furiously,
Shattering all my fortune,
Setting all I had aflame,
I took the keen Albar sword in hand.
Because of all that had befallen,
Because of your ill-fated mother,
A hundred Jediger champions
I struck down wounded.
The black-hearted Kanchoro,
That wicked black devil—
Curse my womanhood!
I failed and struck awry.
My bright eyes dimmed and wandered,
And from the mother who cherished me
I was left alive,
Torn away in disgrace.
The flesh of my right side
Was split apart by a bullet,
Twelve torments and a thousand cruelties
Loomed close above my head.
Sobbing and weeping in grief,
Through unheard-of shame and turmoil,
I was parted from my mother.
I did not spill your blood;
I still bore an uncertain child,
And so I could not bring myself
To take your accursed life.
Wailing shrilly in sorrow,
I was parted from the mother
Who sat cherishing me.
My heart burned and my blood drained,
And all strength left wretched me.
Curse my womanhood!
I have no mountain-high stronghold,
I suffered bitterly—the world is filth.
Curse my womanhood!
I have no strength left to fight.
When I screamed, none heard my voice;
When my true hero was slain,
When my blessed one wrought slaughter,
When they destroyed my gray-maned lord,
They tore away the noble woman,
From the hands of your wretched mother—
